statement: Let $M$ and $N$ be closed, simply connected topological [4-manifolds](c:4-manifold). They are [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) if and only if their [intersection forms](c:intersection-form) are isomorphic and their [Kirby-Siebenmann invariants](c:kirby-siebenmann-invariant) agree. Every unimodular symmetric integral form occurs as such a form, and an odd form occurs with both values of the invariant.

hypotheses.text: The manifolds $M$ and $N$ are closed, connected topological [4-manifolds](c:4-manifold).
The manifolds $M$ and $N$ are [simply connected](c:simply-connected-manifold).

conclusion: The form and the invariant fix the homeomorphism class, every unimodular form occurs, and an even form has one manifold while an odd form has two.

proofs.name: Disc embedding and surgery
proofs.slogan: Realize each form by capping a handlebody with a contractible piece, and join manifolds with equal invariants by an h-cobordism.
proofs.scope: An outline of Freedman's proof; the disc embedding theorem and the surgery step rest on the cited work. For an even form the invariant equals the signature divided by 8, modulo 2, so one manifold remains.

roles.why: Closedness makes the form unimodular by Poincaré duality and allows the capping of a boundary.
The trivial fundamental group gives the homotopy classification by the form and makes 4-dimensional surgery work.

steps.slogan: Show that the [intersection form](c:intersection-form) fixes the homotopy type of the manifold.
steps.detail: Poincaré duality makes the form unimodular. By Milnor and Whitehead, $M$ is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of 2-spheres with one 4-cell attached by a map that the form determines, so isomorphic forms give a homotopy equivalence $M \simeq N$.

steps.slogan: Embed discs in the 4-manifold with the help of [Casson handles](c:casson-handle).
steps.detail: Freedman proves that every Casson handle is homeomorphic to an open 2-handle. This gives the disc embedding theorem for simply connected 4-manifolds, with embedded Whitney discs where the smooth category fails.

steps.slogan: Cap a handlebody with a contractible piece to realize every unimodular form.
steps.detail: A framed link whose linking matrix is $Q$ gives a compact simply connected 4-manifold with boundary a [homology sphere](c:homology-sphere) and form $Q$. Freedman shows that every homology 3-sphere bounds a contractible topological 4-manifold; gluing it in gives a closed manifold with form $Q$.

steps.slogan: Count the values of the [Kirby-Siebenmann invariant](c:kirby-siebenmann-invariant) that each form allows.
steps.detail: The invariant is the obstruction to a PL structure on $M \times \mathbb{R}$, so homeomorphic manifolds share it. For an even form it equals the signature over 8, modulo 2. For an odd form both values occur, for example on $\mathbb{CP}^2$ and on the Chern manifold ${*}\mathbb{CP}^2$.

steps.slogan: Join two manifolds with equal form and invariant by an [h-cobordism](c:h-cobordism).
steps.detail: Step 1 gives a homotopy equivalence, and equal invariants make its normal invariant vanish, so surgery in dimension 4 produces an h-cobordism between $M$ and $N$. The embedded discs of step 2 remove the Whitney obstructions, so the h-cobordism is a product and $M \cong N$.

steps.slogan: Count the manifolds that realize each form to complete the list.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives a manifold for each form, and step 5 shows that equal form and invariant mean homeomorphic. With the values of step 4, an even form has exactly one manifold and an odd form exactly two.

concepts.c:4-manifold: The classification concerns closed simply connected manifolds of dimension four.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The classification is up to homeomorphism, the topological equivalence.
concepts.c:intersection-form: The form on the second homology is the main invariant of the manifold.
concepts.c:kirby-siebenmann-invariant: This second invariant separates the two manifolds that share an odd form.
concepts.c:simply-connected-manifold: Simple connectivity makes the form a complete homotopy invariant.
concepts.c:casson-handle: Casson handles are the objects that Freedman proves to be open 2-handles.
concepts.c:homology-sphere: The boundary of the handlebody is a homology sphere that bounds a contractible piece.
concepts.c:h-cobordism: An h-cobordism joins manifolds with equal invariants and is shown to be a product.

source.ref: M. H. Freedman, The topology of four-dimensional manifolds, Journal of Differential Geometry 17 (1982), 357-453
source.note: Freedman proves existence and uniqueness; M. Freedman and F. Quinn, Topology of 4-manifolds (Princeton, 1990) and the book The Disc Embedding Theorem (Oxford, 2021) give the full account.

statement: Take the advection equation $u_t + a u_x = 0$ and a [linear difference scheme](c:linear-difference-scheme) $u_j^{n+1} = \sum_k c_k u_{j+k}^n$, whose finitely many coefficients depend only on the Courant number $\nu = a\,\Delta t/\Delta x$. If the scheme is [monotone](c:monotone-scheme) and $\nu$ is not an integer, its order of accuracy is at most 1.

hypotheses.text: The scheme is a [linear difference scheme](c:linear-difference-scheme): finitely many coefficients $c_k$ that depend only on $\nu$.
The scheme is [monotone](c:monotone-scheme): larger data give larger new values.
The equation is $u_t + a u_x = 0$ with constant $a \neq 0$, a [hyperbolic PDE](c:hyperbolic-pde).
The Courant number $\nu = a\,\Delta t/\Delta x$ is fixed and is not an integer.

conclusion: The scheme is not second-order accurate: its order of accuracy is at most 1.

new_concepts.name: linear difference scheme
new_concepts.reminder: A finite-difference update that combines grid values with fixed coefficients that do not depend on the data.
new_concepts.definition: A linear difference scheme for a time-dependent equation computes each new grid value as a finite combination $\sum_k c_k u_{j+k}^n$ of old values. The coefficients depend on the mesh ratio but never on the data.

proofs.name: Moment conditions and a sum of squares
proofs.slogan: Second order forces three moment conditions, and monotonicity turns them into a sum of squares that vanishes only for an exact shift.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for a fixed non-integer Courant number. For an integer $\nu$ the scheme can be an exact shift, which is why the hypothesis is needed.

roles.why: Fixed coefficients make the scheme act the same way on all data, so three test solutions give three conditions.
Monotonicity is equivalent to the sign condition $c_k \ge 0$ on every coefficient.
The exact solutions $f(x - at)$ of the equation supply the test values.
A non-integer $\nu$ cannot equal the integer index $-k$.

steps.slogan: Turn [monotonicity](c:monotone-scheme) into the sign condition $c_k \ge 0$ on every coefficient.
steps.detail: Take data equal to $0$ except for the value $1$ at node $j+k$. Monotonicity compares the new value at $j$ with the value for zero data, which is $0$, so $c_k \ge 0$ for every $k$.

steps.slogan: Turn second-order accuracy into three moment conditions on the coefficients.
steps.detail:
The exact solution $u = (x - at)^m$ for $m = 0, 1, 2$ gives the value $(-
u\,\Delta x)^m$ at $x = 0$, $t = \Delta t$, and the [scheme](c:linear-difference-scheme) gives $\Delta x^m \sum_k k^m c_k$. Second order allows an error $O(\Delta x^3)$ only, so $\sum c_k = 1$, $\sum k c_k = -
u$ and $\sum k^2 c_k = 
u^2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the three moments into a weighted sum of squares that equals zero.
steps.detail:
Expand $\sum_k (k + 
u)^2 c_k = \sum k^2 c_k + 2
u \sum k c_k + 
u^2 \sum c_k = 
u^2 - 2
u^2 + 
u^2 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Force every positive coefficient onto the single index $k = -\nu$.
steps.detail: By step 1 each term $(k+\nu)^2 c_k$ is nonnegative, and by step 3 the sum is zero, so each term is zero. Hence $c_k > 0$ implies $k = -\nu$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the integer index when the Courant number is not an integer.
steps.detail:
Since $\sum c_k = 1$, some $c_k > 0$, so $k = -
u$ is an integer. This contradicts $

concepts.c:linear-difference-scheme: Fixed coefficients let one test solution give one condition on the coefficients.
concepts.c:monotone-scheme: Monotonicity gives the sign condition that makes the sum of squares useful.
concepts.c:hyperbolic-pde: The advection equation has exact translated solutions that serve as test data.

source.note: The classical moment argument of Godunov's order barrier theorem (S. K. Godunov, Matematicheskii Sbornik 47 (1959), 271-306), in the form given in the Wikipedia article on Godunov's theorem.

statement: For every integer $k \ge 1$, the [prime numbers](c:prime-number) contain an [arithmetic progression](c:arithmetic-progression) with $k$ terms.

hypotheses.text: The length $k$ is a positive integer.

conclusion: There are positive integers $a$ and $d$ such that $a, a+d, \dots, a+(k-1)d$ are all prime.

proofs.name: Transference to a pseudorandom majorant
proofs.slogan: Dominate the primes by a pseudorandom measure and transfer Szemerédi's theorem from dense sets of integers to dense subsets of that measure.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Green-Tao proof, for $k \ge 3$ (shorter progressions of primes are easy to list). The transference principle and the verification of pseudorandomness rest on the cited paper.

roles.why: The length $k$ fixes the order of Szemerédi's theorem and of the pseudorandom conditions.

steps.slogan: Transfer Szemerédi's theorem to dense subsets of a [pseudorandom measure](c:pseudorandom-measure).
steps.detail: A measure $\nu$ is pseudorandom if its mean is $1 + o(1)$ and it satisfies the linear forms and correlation conditions. Green and Tao show that a function $0 \le f \le \nu$ of mean at least $\delta$ has a positive count of $k$-term progressions, by building a dense model of $f$ and applying Szemerédi's theorem to it.

steps.slogan: Remove the small prime factors with the $W$-trick.
steps.detail: Let $W$ be the product of the primes below a slowly growing bound and $b$ be coprime to $W$. The function $\Lambda_{b,W}(n) = \tfrac{\varphi(W)}{W}\Lambda(Wn+b)$ has mean $1 + o(1)$ over $n \le N$, by the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions, so it is dense.

steps.slogan: Dominate the shifted primes by a measure built from a [sieve](c:selberg-sieve).
steps.detail: Following Goldston and Yıldırım, take for $\nu(n)$ the normalized square of the truncated divisor sum $\sum_{d \mid Wn+b,\, d \le R} \mu(d)\log(R/d)$. This is a Selberg-type sieve weight, and it bounds $\Lambda_{b,W}$ by a constant multiple of $\nu$.

steps.slogan: Verify that the sieve measure $\nu$ is [pseudorandom](c:pseudorandom-measure).
steps.detail: The linear forms and correlation conditions reduce to averages of divisor sums over several linear forms. Green and Tao evaluate them with the Goldston-Yıldırım method, using contour integrals and the zeta function, so $\nu$ is pseudorandom.

steps.slogan: Apply the transfer to $\Lambda_{b,W}$ to find a long progression of primes.
steps.detail: The function $\Lambda_{b,W}/C \le \nu$ has positive mean, so step 1 gives a $k$-term progression $n, n+r, \dots$ on which it is positive. Up to prime powers, which are rare, the numbers $Wn+b, W(n+r)+b, \dots$ are primes in a progression of difference $Wr$.

concepts.c:prime-number: The primes are the set in which the progression is found.
concepts.c:arithmetic-progression: The theorem asks for progressions of every length inside the primes.
concepts.c:pseudorandom-measure: The measure that majorizes the primes must be pseudorandom for the transfer to work.
concepts.c:selberg-sieve: A Selberg-type sieve weight supplies the majorant of the shifted primes.

source.ref: B. Green and T. Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Annals of Mathematics 167 (2008), 481-547
source.note: The steps follow the three parts of the paper: the transference principle, the W-trick with the sieve majorant, and the pseudorandomness estimates.

statement: Let $f\colon X \to Y$ be a [proper morphism](c:is-proper) of [Noetherian schemes](c:is-noetherian). The [derived direct image](c:derived-direct-image) $Rf_*\colon D_{qc}(X) \to D_{qc}(Y)$ between [derived categories](c:derived-category) of [quasicoherent sheaves](c:quasicoherent-sheaf) has a [right adjoint](c:is-right-adjoint) $f^!$.

hypotheses.text: The schemes $X$ and $Y$ are [Noetherian](c:is-noetherian).
The morphism $f$ is [proper](c:is-proper).

conclusion: A functor $f^!\colon D_{qc}(Y) \to D_{qc}(X)$ exists with natural isomorphisms $\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_*F, G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(F, f^!G)$.

proofs.name: Brown representability
proofs.slogan: Show that $Rf_*$ preserves sums on a compactly generated category, then obtain the right adjoint from Brown representability.
proofs.scope: An outline of Neeman's proof, which needs only that $f$ is separated and quasi-compact. Its identification with Hartshorne's dualizing functor on bounded below complexes rests on the cited work.

roles.why: Noetherian schemes are quasi-compact and quasi-separated, so $D_{qc}$ is well behaved and compactly generated.
A proper morphism is separated and quasi-compact, so pushforward keeps quasicoherence and preserves sums.

steps.slogan: Check that $Rf_*$ sends [quasicoherent](c:quasicoherent-sheaf) complexes to quasicoherent complexes.
steps.detail: A proper morphism of Noetherian schemes is quasi-compact and separated, so $R^if_*$ of a quasicoherent sheaf is quasicoherent. Hence $Rf_*$ restricts to a triangulated functor $D_{qc}(X) \to D_{qc}(Y)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the quasicoherent derived category has compact generators.
steps.detail: For a quasi-compact separated scheme the perfect complexes are compact objects, and a single perfect complex generates (Thomason-Trobaugh, Bondal-van den Bergh, Neeman). So $D_{qc}(X)$ is a [compactly generated triangulated category](c:compactly-generated-triangulated-category).

steps.slogan: Show that $Rf_*$ preserves arbitrary direct sums.
steps.detail: Compute $Rf_*$ with a finite affine Čech cover of $X$. Cohomology of quasicoherent sheaves on affine schemes commutes with direct sums, so $Rf_*$ commutes with them as well.

steps.slogan: Represent the functor $F \mapsto \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_*F, G)$ by an object $f^!G$.
steps.detail: For fixed $G$ the functor is cohomological and turns direct sums into products. By Neeman's form of Brown representability for compactly generated categories it is represented by an object $f^!G$ of $D_{qc}(X)$, and the representing objects are functorial in $G$.

steps.slogan: Assemble the representing objects into the [right adjoint](c:is-right-adjoint) $f^!$.
steps.detail: The natural isomorphisms $\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_*F, G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}(F, f^!G)$ make $f^!$ a functor on $D_{qc}(Y)$ that is right adjoint to $Rf_*$. On bounded below complexes it agrees with the functor that Hartshorne constructs in Residues and Duality.

concepts.c:is-proper: Properness makes pushforward keep quasicoherence and preserve sums.
concepts.c:is-noetherian: The Noetherian hypothesis gives quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes.
concepts.c:derived-direct-image: The derived direct image is the functor whose right adjoint is constructed.
concepts.c:derived-category: The adjoint lives between the derived categories of quasicoherent sheaves.
concepts.c:quasicoherent-sheaf: Quasicoherent complexes form the categories on which the adjoint is built.
concepts.c:is-right-adjoint: The conclusion is the existence of this right adjoint.
concepts.c:compactly-generated-triangulated-categ: Compact generation is what Brown representability requires of the source.

source.ref: A. Neeman, The Grothendieck duality theorem via Bousfield's techniques and Brown representability, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 9 (1996), 205-236
source.note: Neeman gives the existence of the adjoint through Brown representability; R. Hartshorne, Residues and Duality (Springer LNM 20, 1966) is the original construction.

statement: Let $X$ be a separated scheme of finite type over a [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $\ell$ a prime not dividing $q$. For every $n \ge 1$, $\#X(\mathbb{F}_{q^n}) = \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{Tr}(F^n \mid H^i_c(X_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell))$, where $F$ is the geometric [Frobenius](c:frobenius) and $H^i_c$ is compactly supported [étale cohomology](c:etale-cohomology).

hypotheses.text: The scheme $X$ is separated and of finite type over $\mathbb{F}_q$.
The prime $\ell$ does not divide $q$.
The exponent $n$ is a positive integer.

conclusion: The number of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$-points of $X$ is the alternating sum of the [traces](c:trace-of-a-matrix) of $F^n$ on compactly supported $\ell$-adic cohomology.

proofs.name: Reduction to curves and the Lefschetz formula
proofs.slogan: Count points as fixed points of Frobenius, reduce to curves by fibrations, and prove the curve case with the Lefschetz fixed point formula.
proofs.scope: An outline of Grothendieck's proof as written by Deligne; applied to $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$ it reduces the theorem to $n = 1$. The curve case and the passage to $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ rest on the cited work.

roles.why: Replacing $q$ by $q^n$ reduces the formula for $F^n$ to the case $n = 1$.
Separated of finite type gives finite compactly supported cohomology and a fibration of $X$ by curves.
An invertible $\ell$ gives $\ell$-adic cohomology with proper base change and duality.

steps.slogan: Identify the rational points with the fixed points of [Frobenius](c:frobenius).
steps.detail: The set $X(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})$ is the set of points of $X(\bar{\mathbb{F}}_q)$ fixed by $F^n$. Since $F^n$ is the Frobenius of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}$, one may replace $q$ by $q^n$ and take $n = 1$.

steps.slogan: State the formula for constructible $\ell$-adic sheaves so that induction on dimension works.
steps.detail: For a constructible sheaf $\mathcal{F}$ the formula equates $\sum_{x \in X(\mathbb{F}_q)} \operatorname{Tr}(F_x \mid \mathcal{F}_x)$ with the alternating trace on compactly supported [étale cohomology](c:etale-cohomology) of $\mathcal{F}$. Both sides are additive in $\mathcal{F}$ and in a decomposition of $X$ into closed and open parts.

steps.slogan: Reduce the formula to curves by fibrations and proper base change.
steps.detail: Fibering $X$ by curves over a base $Y$ of smaller dimension, the fiber of $Rf_!\mathcal{F}$ at a point $y$ is $R\Gamma_c(X_y, \mathcal{F})$ by proper base change. The curve case on the fibers and the formula on $Y$ for the sheaf $Rf_!\mathcal{F}$ then give the formula on $X$.

steps.slogan: Prove the curve case from the Lefschetz fixed point formula for Frobenius.
steps.detail: On a smooth projective curve the $\ell$-adic Lefschetz-Verdier formula equates the alternating trace of an endomorphism with its fixed-point count. For Frobenius the graph meets the diagonal transversally, since $dF = 0$, so each fixed point counts once. Poincaré duality and dévissage handle the affine curve with a lisse sheaf.

steps.slogan: Pass from torsion coefficients to $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ to obtain the stated formula.
steps.detail: The formula holds for coefficients $\mathbb{Z}/\ell^m$ on perfect complexes, hence in the limit for $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$-sheaves. Tensoring with $\mathbb{Q}_\ell$ gives the trace formula on $H^i_c(X_{\bar{\mathbb{F}}_q}, \mathbb{Q}_\ell)$, and step 1 gives all $n$.

concepts.c:finite-field: The variety is defined over a finite field, which makes its points countable.
concepts.c:frobenius: The Frobenius endomorphism has the rational points as its fixed points.
concepts.c:etale-cohomology: Compactly supported étale cohomology carries the action whose trace is taken.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: Traces of Frobenius on the cohomology groups appear in the alternating sum.

source.ref: P. Deligne, Rapport sur la formule des traces, in Cohomologie étale (SGA 4 1/2), Lecture Notes in Mathematics 569, Springer, 1977, pp. 76-109
source.note: The Rapport gives the complete proof of the trace formula for Frobenius, following Grothendieck's argument in SGA 5.

statement: Let $M$ be an [open manifold](c:open-manifold) and $R$ an open, $\mathrm{Diff}(M)$-invariant differential relation, that is, an open subset of the [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle) $X^{(r)}$ of a natural bundle $X \to M$. Every formal solution of $R$ is homotopic, through formal solutions, to a [holonomic section](c:holonomic-section), which is the jet of a genuine solution.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is [open](c:open-manifold): it has no compact component.
The relation $R$ is an open subset of the [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle) $X^{(r)}$.
The relation $R$ is invariant under the [diffeomorphisms](c:diffeomorph) of $M$, which act on the natural bundle $X$.

conclusion: Each section of $R$ is homotopic through sections of $R$ to the $r$-jet of a section of $X$.

proofs.name: Holonomic approximation on a skeleton
proofs.slogan: Push the manifold into a neighborhood of a codimension-one polyhedron, make the formal solution holonomic there, and pull the result back.
proofs.scope: An outline of the Eliashberg-Mishachev proof of Gromov's theorem for open Diff-invariant relations. The holonomic approximation theorem, which carries the main work, rests on the cited book.

roles.why: An [open manifold](c:open-manifold) can be pushed into a neighborhood of a polyhedron of positive codimension.
Openness keeps every section that is close to a formal solution inside $R$.
Invariance lets the solution pulled back by a diffeomorphism stay in $R$.

steps.slogan: Find a polyhedron of positive codimension that carries the [open manifold](c:open-manifold).
steps.detail: An open manifold has a handle decomposition without top handles, so it deformation retracts to a polyhedron $K$ of dimension at most $n-1$. For every neighborhood $U$ of $K$ there is a diffeotopy $h_t$ of $M$ with $h_1(M) \subset U$.

steps.slogan: Make the formal solution holonomic near the polyhedron by holonomic approximation.
steps.detail: The holonomic approximation theorem gives, for a section $F_0$ of the [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle) near $K$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, a small diffeotopy of $K$ and a [holonomic section](c:holonomic-section) $F_1$ near the moved polyhedron that is $\varepsilon$-close to $F_0$ in $C^0$.

steps.slogan: Keep the approximating section inside the open relation $R$.
steps.detail: Because $R$ is open and $F_0$ is continuous with values in $R$, a small enough $\varepsilon$ puts every $\varepsilon$-close section in $R$. So $F_1$ is a genuine solution of $R$ near the moved polyhedron, and a short homotopy joins $F_0$ to $F_1$ through sections of $R$.

steps.slogan: Pull the solution back to all of $M$ by the diffeotopy.
steps.detail: Choose $U$ and $h_t$ so that $h_1(M)$ lies in the domain of $F_1$. Because $R$ is invariant under [diffeomorphisms](c:diffeomorph), the pullback of $F_1$ by $h_1$ is a holonomic section of $R$ over $M$, and pulling back the homotopy and the isotopy joins it to $F_0$.

concepts.c:open-manifold: Openness gives a polyhedron of positive codimension that carries the manifold.
concepts.c:jet-bundle: Formal and holonomic solutions are sections of the jet bundle.
concepts.c:holonomic-section: The genuine solution is a holonomic section: the jet of a section.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: Diffeomorphism invariance of the relation allows the final pullback.

source.ref: Y. Eliashberg and N. Mishachev, Introduction to the h-Principle, Graduate Studies in Mathematics 48, American Mathematical Society, 2002
source.note: Holonomic approximation and its use for open Diff-invariant relations are in this book; M. Gromov, Partial Differential Relations (Springer, 1986) proves the theorem in general form.

statement: Let $E$ be a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) on a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) $C$. Then $E$ has a unique [filtration](c:filtration) $0 = E_0 \subset E_1 \subset \dots \subset E_m = E$ by subbundles whose quotients $E_i/E_{i-1}$ are semistable ([slope stability](c:slope-stability)) with strictly decreasing [slopes](c:slope-of-a-coherent-sheaf).

hypotheses.text: The curve $C$ is a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) over a field.
The sheaf $E$ is a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) on $C$.

conclusion: A filtration by subbundles with semistable quotients of strictly decreasing slope exists and is unique.

proofs.name: Maximal destabilizing subbundle
proofs.slogan: Take the subsheaf of maximal slope and maximal rank, show that it is unique and saturated, and repeat on the quotient.
proofs.scope: The case $E \neq 0$, by induction on the rank; for $E = 0$ the filtration is empty. Semistable means $\mu(F) \le \mu(E)$ for every nonzero subsheaf $F$, where the slope is $\mu = \deg/\operatorname{rank}$.

roles.why: On a smooth curve a torsion-free sheaf is locally free, and degrees of subsheaves are bounded.
A bundle has finite rank, so slopes lie in a discrete set and induction on the rank ends.

steps.slogan: Bound the [slopes](c:slope-of-a-coherent-sheaf) of the nonzero subsheaves of $E$ from above.
steps.detail: A subsheaf $F \subset E$ of rank $r$ is a vector bundle, and $\det F \to \wedge^r E$ is a nonzero map. Embedding $\wedge^r E$ in a sum of copies of $\mathcal{O}(m)$ bounds the [degree](c:degree-of-a-coherent-sheaf) of $\det F$ by a constant that depends on $E$ and $r$. So the slopes are bounded above.

steps.slogan: Choose the subsheaf $E_1$ of maximal slope and, among those, of maximal rank.
steps.detail: Slopes lie in the discrete set $\frac{1}{r}\mathbb{Z}$ with $r \le \operatorname{rank} E$, so a maximal slope $\mu_1$ is attained. If $F$ also has slope $\mu_1$, then $\deg(E_1 + F) = \deg E_1 + \deg F - \deg(E_1 \cap F)$ gives slope at least $\mu_1$, so $E_1 + F = E_1$ by maximality of rank. Hence $E_1$ is unique and contains every subsheaf of slope $\mu_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $E_1$ is a semistable subbundle.
steps.detail: Every subsheaf of $E_1$ has slope at most $\mu_1$, so $E_1$ is semistable ([slope stability](c:slope-stability)). The saturation of $E_1$ has slope at least $\mu_1$, so it lies in $E_1$ by step 2. Hence $E/E_1$ is torsion free, so it is a vector bundle.

steps.slogan: Show that the quotient bundle has all slopes below $\mu_1$.
steps.detail: Let $G \subset E/E_1$ be nonzero with preimage $G' \subset E$. Then $\deg G' = \deg E_1 + \deg G$ and the ranks add, so $\mu(G) \ge \mu_1$ would give $\mu(G') \ge \mu_1$ with $\operatorname{rank} G' > \operatorname{rank} E_1$, against the choice of $E_1$. So $\mu(G) < \mu_1$.

steps.slogan: Build the filtration by induction on the rank.
steps.detail: The bundle $E/E_1$ has smaller rank, so it has a filtration with semistable quotients of strictly decreasing slopes, all below $\mu_1$ by step 4. Pulling this filtration back to $E$ and putting $E_1$ first gives the required filtration.

steps.slogan: Show that every such filtration begins with $E_1$, so the filtration is unique.
steps.detail: Let $E'_i$ be another such filtration. For a subsheaf $F \subset E$, the pieces $F \cap E'_i / F \cap E'_{i-1}$ lie in semistable quotients of slope $\mu'_i \le \mu'_1$, so $\mu(F) \le \mu'_1$ with equality only if $F \subset E'_1$; hence $\mu'_1 = \mu_1$ and $E'_1 = E_1$ by step 2. The quotient filtrations agree by induction on the rank.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: On a smooth curve, torsion-free sheaves are bundles and degrees behave well.
concepts.c:vector-bundle: The theorem filters a vector bundle by subbundles.
concepts.c:filtration: The result is a filtration with semistable graded pieces.
concepts.c:slope-stability: Semistability of the pieces is what the maximal subsheaf has.
concepts.c:slope-of-a-coherent-sheaf: Slopes order the subsheaves and decrease along the filtration.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-coherent-sheaf: Bounded degrees give bounded slopes of subsheaves.

source.note: The classical argument of G. Harder and M. S. Narasimhan, Mathematische Annalen 212 (1975), 215-248, as presented in Huybrechts and Lehn, The Geometry of Moduli Spaces of Sheaves, section 1.3.

statement: Let $\omega(n)$ be the number of distinct [prime](c:prime-number) factors of $n$. For every $\varepsilon > 0$, the number of $n \le x$ with $|\omega(n) - \log\log n| > \varepsilon \log\log n$ is $o(x)$ as $x \to \infty$. So $\log\log n$ is the [normal order](c:normal-order-of-an-arithmetic-function) of the [arithmetic function](c:arithmetic-function) $\omega$.

hypotheses.text: The tolerance $\varepsilon > 0$ is fixed.

conclusion: Almost all positive integers $n$ satisfy $|\omega(n) - \log\log n| \le \varepsilon \log\log n$.

new_concepts.name: normal order of an arithmetic function
new_concepts.reminder: A function $g$ is a normal order of an arithmetic function $f$ if $f(n)$ is close to $g(n)$ for almost all $n$.
new_concepts.definition: A function $g$ is a normal order of the [arithmetic function](c:arithmetic-function) $f$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the number of $n \le x$ with $|f(n) - g(n)| > \varepsilon g(n)$ is $o(x)$ as $x \to \infty$.

proofs.name: Turán's variance bound
proofs.slogan: Bound the variance of the number of small prime factors, then apply Chebyshev's inequality and return to $\omega$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for fixed $\varepsilon$ and large $x$. The integers $n \le \sqrt{x}$ are set aside because there are few of them.

roles.why: The tolerance sets the threshold in Chebyshev's inequality and the final comparison.

steps.slogan: Count only the prime factors below $y = x^{1/10}$.
steps.detail: Let $\omega_y(n)$ count the [primes](c:prime-number) $p \le y$ that divide $n$. For $n \le x$, at most 9 distinct primes above $y$ divide $n$, because 10 of them would multiply to more than $y^{10} = x$. So $0 \le \omega(n) - \omega_y(n) \le 9$.

steps.slogan: Compute the first two moments of $\omega_y$ over the integers $n \le x$.
steps.detail: Put $\mu = \sum_{p \le y} 1/p$, so $\mu = \log\log x + O(1)$ by Mertens. Counting pairs of primes that divide $n$ gives $\sum_{n \le x}\omega_y(n) = \sum_p \lfloor x/p \rfloor \ge x\mu - y$ and $\sum_{n \le x}\omega_y(n)^2 = \sum_{p \ne q}\lfloor x/pq \rfloor + \sum_p \lfloor x/p \rfloor \le x\mu^2 + x\mu$.

steps.slogan: Combine the moments into a bound on the [variance](c:variance).
steps.detail: Expanding, $\sum_{n \le x}(\omega_y(n) - \mu)^2 = \sum \omega_y^2 - 2\mu\sum\omega_y + \mu^2\lfloor x \rfloor \le x\mu + 2\mu y$. With $y = x^{1/10}$ this is at most $3x\log\log x$ for large $x$. It is the case $f = \omega$ of the Turán-Kubilius inequality.

steps.slogan: Count the integers whose truncated count is far from $\mu$.
steps.detail: Put $L = \log\log x$. By Chebyshev's inequality for the counting measure on $n \le x$, at most $3xL/(\varepsilon L/2)^2 = 12x/(\varepsilon^2 L)$ integers $n \le x$ have $|\omega_y(n) - \mu| > \varepsilon L/2$. This number is $o(x)$.

steps.slogan: Return from $\omega_y$ and $\mu$ to $\omega$ and $\log\log n$.
steps.detail: For $\sqrt{x} < n \le x$ we have $|\log\log n - L| \le \log 2$, $|\mu - L| \le C$ and $|\omega(n) - \omega_y(n)| \le 9$. If $|\omega_y(n) - \mu| \le \varepsilon L/2$ and $x$ is large, then $|\omega(n) - \log\log n| \le \varepsilon L/2 + 9 + C + \log 2 \le \varepsilon \log\log n$. So at most $\sqrt{x} + 12x/(\varepsilon^2 L) = o(x)$ integers $n \le x$ are exceptional.

concepts.c:prime-number: The function $\omega$ counts distinct prime factors, and the proof sums over primes.
concepts.c:normal-order-of-an-arithmetic-function: The theorem says that $\log\log n$ is the normal order of $\omega$.
concepts.c:arithmetic-function: The function $\omega$ is an arithmetic function studied through its typical size.
concepts.c:variance: A bound on the variance of $\omega_y$ forces most values near the mean.

source.note: Turán's variance proof, P. Turán, On a theorem of Hardy and Ramanujan, Journal of the London Mathematical Society 9 (1934), 274-276; the theorem is from Hardy and Ramanujan, Quarterly Journal of Mathematics 48 (1917), 76-92.

statement: Let $\lambda$ be an [integer partition](c:integer-partition) and $n \ge 1$. The number of [semistandard Young tableaux](c:semistandard-young-tableau) of shape $\lambda$ with entries in $\{1, \dots, n\}$ is $\prod_{u \in \lambda} \frac{n + c(u)}{h(u)}$, where $c(u) = j - i$ is the content and $h(u)$ the hook length of the cell $u = (i,j)$ of the [Young diagram](c:young-diagram).

hypotheses.text: The shape $\lambda$ is an [integer partition](c:integer-partition) with Young diagram $\{(i,j) : 1 \le j \le \lambda_i\}$.
The entries come from the alphabet $\{1, \dots, n\}$ with $n \ge 1$.

conclusion: The number of such tableaux is the product over the cells $u$ of $(n + c(u))/h(u)$.

proofs.name: Principal specialization of the Schur polynomial
proofs.slogan: Write the count as a Schur polynomial at $x = (1, \dots, 1)$, evaluate it as a limit of Vandermonde ratios, and convert the product to hooks and contents.
proofs.scope: The case $n \ge \ell(\lambda)$, the number of rows; for $n < \ell(\lambda)$ both sides are 0, since the cell $(n+1, 1)$ gives the factor $n + c = 0$. Write $l_i = \lambda_i + n - i$ for $1 \le i \le n$.

roles.why: The cells of the diagram give the contents and the hook lengths of each row.
The alphabet size $n$ is the number of variables of the Schur polynomial.

steps.slogan: Write the tableau count as the [Schur polynomial](c:schur-polynomial) $s_\lambda(1^n)$.
steps.detail: The Schur polynomial $s_\lambda(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ is the sum of $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_n^{a_n}$ over [semistandard tableaux](c:semistandard-young-tableau) of shape $\lambda$, where $a_i$ counts the entries equal to $i$. Setting every $x_i = 1$ counts the tableaux.

steps.slogan: Express the Schur polynomial as a ratio of two alternating determinants.
steps.detail: The classical equivalence of the tableau definition and the bialternant formula gives $s_\lambda = \det(x_i^{l_j}) / \det(x_i^{n-j})$.

steps.slogan: Specialize to powers of $q$ and let $q \to 1$ to get a product of differences.
steps.detail: Setting $x_i = q^{n-i}$ turns both determinants into [Vandermonde determinants](c:vandermonde-determinant), so $s_\lambda(q^{n-1}, \dots, 1) = \prod_{i<j} \frac{q^{l_i} - q^{l_j}}{q^{n-i} - q^{n-j}}$. Each factor tends to $(l_i - l_j)/(j - i)$ as $q \to 1$, so $s_\lambda(1^n) = \prod_{i<j} \frac{l_i - l_j}{j - i}$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the product of the contents as factorials.
steps.detail: In row $i$ the contents are $1 - i, \dots, \lambda_i - i$, so $\prod_{u \in \text{row } i}(n + c(u)) = (n - i + 1)\cdots(n - i + \lambda_i) = l_i!/(n-i)!$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the product of the hook lengths through the numbers $l_i$.
steps.detail: Encode the boundary of the [Young diagram](c:young-diagram) by the positions $l_1 > \dots > l_n \ge 0$ of its vertical steps. The hook lengths of row $i$ are the distances from $l_i$ to the horizontal steps below it, and the distances to the vertical steps below are the $l_i - l_j$ with $j > i$. All of $1, \dots, l_i$ occur once, so $\prod_{u \in \text{row } i} h(u) = l_i! / \prod_{j > i}(l_i - l_j)$.

steps.slogan: Divide the two products and compare the result with the limit formula.
steps.detail: The ratio is $\prod_u \frac{n + c(u)}{h(u)} = \prod_i \frac{l_i!}{(n-i)!} \cdot \frac{\prod_{j>i}(l_i - l_j)}{l_i!} = \frac{\prod_{i<j}(l_i - l_j)}{\prod_i (n-i)!}$. Since $\prod_{i<j}(j - i) = \prod_i (n-i)!$, this equals $s_\lambda(1^n)$ from step 3, which is the tableau count of step 1.

concepts.c:integer-partition: The partition $\lambda$ is the shape that fixes the diagram and the rows.
concepts.c:semistandard-young-tableau: The semistandard tableaux are the objects that the formula counts.
concepts.c:young-diagram: Contents and hook lengths are measured on the cells of the diagram.
concepts.c:schur-polynomial: The Schur polynomial at all ones equals the tableau count.
concepts.c:vandermonde-determinant: The specialized alternants are Vandermonde determinants with a product formula.

source.note: The principal specialization proof of the hook-content formula, as in Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, volume 2, section 7.21.

statement: Let $M$ be a connected [closed oriented manifold](c:closed-oriented-manifold) of dimension $n \ge 1$, smooth. Two maps $M \to S^n$ are [homotopic](c:homotopy) if and only if they have the same [degree](c:degree-of-a-map), and every integer is the degree of some map.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is a connected, smooth, [closed oriented manifold](c:closed-oriented-manifold) of dimension $n$.
The dimension satisfies $n \ge 1$.

conclusion: The degree is a bijection from the homotopy classes of maps $M \to S^n$ to $\mathbb{Z}$.

proofs.name: Comparison with an Eilenberg-MacLane space
proofs.slogan: Maps from an $n$-dimensional complex to $S^n$ and to $K(\mathbb{Z}, n)$ have the same homotopy classes, and the classes into $K(\mathbb{Z}, n)$ form the cohomology group $H^n$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for a smooth $M$, which is triangulable. The sphere is $(n-1)$-connected, which is why $n \ge 1$ is enough.

roles.why: Triangulability gives an $n$-dimensional complex, and the fundamental class gives $H^n(M) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
For $n \ge 1$ the sphere is connected and $\pi_n(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, so cells of dimension at least $n+2$ finish the model.

steps.slogan: Give the manifold a CW structure of dimension $n$.
steps.detail: A smooth closed manifold is triangulable by Whitehead's theorem, so $M$ is a finite [CW complex](c:cw-complex) with cells of dimension at most $n$.

steps.slogan: Build $K(\mathbb{Z}, n)$ from $S^n$ by attaching cells of dimension at least $n+2$.
steps.detail: The sphere $S^n$ is $(n-1)$-connected with $\pi_n(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ by the Hurewicz theorem. Attaching $(n+2)$-cells kills $\pi_{n+1}$ and higher cells kill the rest, which gives an [Eilenberg-Mac Lane space](c:eilenberg-mac-lane-space) $K$. The pair $(K, S^n)$ is then $(n+1)$-connected.

steps.slogan: Compress maps and homotopies from $M$ into the sphere.
steps.detail: Since $\dim M \le n$ and $(K, S^n)$ is $(n+1)$-connected, cellular approximation and the compression lemma deform every map $M \to K$ into $S^n$. They do the same for a homotopy $M \times I \to K$, of dimension at most $n+1$, between maps into $S^n$. So $[M, S^n] \to [M, K]$ is a bijection.

steps.slogan: Identify the homotopy classes into $K$ with the cohomology group $H^n(M; \mathbb{Z})$.
steps.detail: By Brown representability, $g \mapsto g^*\iota$ is a bijection from $[M, K]$ to $H^n(M; \mathbb{Z})$, where $\iota$ is the fundamental class of $K$. Its restriction to $S^n$ is a generator $\sigma$ of $H^n(S^n)$, so a map $f\colon M \to S^n$ goes to $f^*\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Read the [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) off the [fundamental class](c:fundamental-class) of $M$.
steps.detail: Because $M$ is closed, connected and oriented, evaluation on $[M]$ gives an isomorphism $H^n(M; \mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}$, and $\deg f = \langle f^*\sigma, [M] \rangle$. So the homotopy classes of maps $M \to S^n$ correspond bijectively to $\mathbb{Z}$ by the degree.

concepts.c:closed-oriented-manifold: Closedness and orientation give a fundamental class that defines the degree.
concepts.c:homotopy: The theorem classifies maps up to homotopy.
concepts.c:degree-of-a-map: The degree is the complete invariant of the homotopy class.
concepts.c:cw-complex: A CW structure of dimension $n$ allows cellular approximation and compression.
concepts.c:eilenberg-mac-lane-space: The space $K(\mathbb{Z}, n)$ represents cohomology and agrees with the sphere in low dimensions.
concepts.c:fundamental-class: Evaluation on the fundamental class turns a cohomology class into an integer.

source.note: Hopf's theorem (1926) by comparison with K(Z,n), as in Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, chapter 4; the smooth proof by framed cobordism is in Milnor, Topology from the Differentiable Viewpoint.

statement: For every [irrational](c:irrational-number) $\xi$ there are infinitely many coprime pairs $(m, n)$ with $n \ge 1$ and $|\xi - m/n| < 1/(\sqrt{5}\,n^2)$. The constant $\sqrt{5}$ is best possible: for the [golden ratio](c:golden-ratio) $\xi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$ and any $A > \sqrt{5}$, only finitely many pairs satisfy $|\xi - m/n| < 1/(A n^2)$.

hypotheses.text: The number $\xi$ is an [irrational](c:irrational-number) real number.

conclusion: Infinitely many coprime fractions approximate $\xi$ within $1/(\sqrt{5}\,n^2)$, and no larger constant works for all irrationals.

proofs.name: Three consecutive convergents
proofs.slogan: Among any three consecutive convergents of the continued fraction one meets the bound, and the golden ratio shows that the constant is sharp.
proofs.scope: Both parts: existence for an arbitrary irrational, and sharpness at the golden ratio $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2$. The existence part uses the convergents $p_k/q_k$ with $k \ge 1$.

roles.why: Irrationality gives an infinite [continued fraction](c:continued-fraction) with infinitely many distinct convergents.

steps.slogan: Write the error of a convergent through the complete quotients.
steps.detail: Let $p_k/q_k$ be the convergents of $\xi = [a_0; a_1, \dots]$ (see [continued fraction](c:continued-fraction)), $\xi_{k+1} > 1$ the complete quotients and $r_k = q_{k-1}/q_k$. Then $q_k^2 |\xi - p_k/q_k| = 1/(\xi_{k+1} + r_k)$. So the bound fails at $k$ exactly when $\xi_{k+1} + r_k \le \sqrt{5}$; call this failure $F_k$.

steps.slogan: Link consecutive failures through the identity $\xi_k + r_{k-1} = 1/r_k + 1/\xi_{k+1}$.
steps.detail: From $\xi_k = a_k + 1/\xi_{k+1}$ and $1/r_k = a_k + r_{k-1}$ the identity follows. With $x = 1/\xi_{k+1}$ and $y = r_k$, the failures $F_{k-1}$ and $F_k$ read $x + 1/y \le \sqrt{5}$ and $1/x + y \le \sqrt{5}$.

steps.slogan: Show that two consecutive failures force $\xi_{k+1} \le \varphi$.
steps.detail: The two inequalities give $y \ge 1/(\sqrt{5} - x)$ and $1/x \le \sqrt{5} - y$, so $x(\sqrt{5} - x) \ge 1$, that is, $x^2 - \sqrt{5}\,x + 1 \le 0$. Since $x < 1$, this gives $x \ge 1/\varphi$, so $\xi_{k+1} \le \varphi$.

steps.slogan: Show that three consecutive failures are impossible.
steps.detail: If $F_{k-1}, F_k, F_{k+1}$ hold, then $\xi_{k+1} \le \varphi$ and $\xi_{k+2} \le \varphi$, so $\xi_{k+1} = a_{k+1} + 1/\xi_{k+2} \ge 1 + 1/\varphi = \varphi$ and $\xi_{k+1} = \varphi$. Then $F_{k-1}$ and $F_k$ give $y = 1/\varphi$, which is irrational, while $y = q_{k-1}/q_k$ is rational.

steps.slogan: Prove sharpness with the golden ratio and the integer $m^2 - mn - n^2$.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi' = (1 - \sqrt{5})/2$. Then $m^2 - mn - n^2 = (m - n\varphi)(m - n\varphi')$ is a nonzero integer, so its absolute value is at least 1. If $|\varphi - m/n| < 1/(An^2)$, the product is below $\frac{1}{An}\big(n\sqrt{5} + \frac{1}{An}\big)$, which tends to $\sqrt{5}/A < 1$; so $n$ is bounded and only finitely many pairs exist.

steps.slogan: Collect infinitely many distinct convergents and join them with the sharpness bound.
steps.detail: The triples $(k-1, k, k+1)$ for $k = 1, 4, 7, \dots$ are disjoint, and each holds a convergent that meets the bound. Convergents are distinct reduced fractions because $q_k$ increases, so infinitely many pairs exist. Together with step 5 this proves both parts.

concepts.c:irrational-number: Irrationality gives infinitely many convergents and the contradiction with a rational $r_k$.
concepts.c:golden-ratio: The golden ratio is the extremal number for which the constant is sharp.
concepts.c:continued-fraction: The convergents of the continued fraction supply the approximating fractions.

source.note: The convergent argument of A. Hurwitz, Mathematische Annalen 39 (1891), 279-284, in the form found in Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, chapter 11.

statement: Let $a \le b$ and let $f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function). Then $f([a, b])$ is the [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[m, M]$, where $m$ and $M$ are the minimum and the maximum of $f$ on $[a, b]$.

hypotheses.text: The endpoints satisfy $a \le b$, so the [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[a, b]$ is nonempty.
The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a, b]$.

conclusion: The image equals $[\inf f([a,b]), \sup f([a,b])]$, and both endpoints are values of $f$.

formal.difference: mathlib proves it for a densely ordered, conditionally complete domain and a conditionally complete codomain, both with the order topology, not only for $\mathbb{R}$. Its equation $f''[a,b] = [\mathrm{sInf}, \mathrm{sSup}]$ contains the attainment of both endpoints.

proofs.name: Connected and compact image
proofs.slogan: The image is connected and compact, so it is an interval that contains its infimum and supremum.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The hypothesis $a \le b$ is used only to make the image nonempty.

roles.why: A nonempty interval has a nonempty image, so the infimum and supremum exist.
A continuous map keeps both connectedness and compactness.

steps.slogan: Push the connected interval forward to a connected image.
steps.detail: The interval $[a, b]$ is a [connected space](c:connected-space). A continuous image of a connected space is connected, so $f([a,b])$ is a connected set of reals, and it is nonempty because $a \le b$.

steps.slogan: Push the compact interval forward to a compact image.
steps.detail: By the Heine-Borel theorem $[a, b]$ is [compact](c:compact-space). The continuous image of a compact space is compact, so $f([a,b])$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the image contains its infimum and its supremum.
steps.detail: A nonempty bounded set of reals has an infimum $m$ and a supremum $M$ (see [least upper bound](c:least-upper-bound)). Both lie in the closure of the image, which is the image itself because it is closed. So $m$ and $M$ are values of $f$.

steps.slogan: Fill the gap between $m$ and $M$ by connectedness.
steps.detail: A connected set of reals is an interval, so the image contains every $t$ with $m \le t \le M$, because $m$ and $M$ are in it. The image lies in $[m, M]$ by the definition of infimum and supremum, so the image equals $[m, M]$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity is what makes the image connected and compact.
concepts.c:closed-interval: The domain and the image are closed intervals.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness of the image makes it an interval with no gaps.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the image gives closed and bounded, so the ends are attained.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum and infimum of the image are the endpoints of the interval.

source.note: mathlib shows that the image is connected (isPreconnected_Icc.image) and compact (isCompact_Icc.image_of_continuousOn), then applies eq_Icc_of_connected_compact.

proofs.name: Extreme and intermediate value theorems
proofs.slogan: Attain the minimum and maximum by the extreme value theorem, then fill the values between them by the intermediate value theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If the minimum and maximum points coincide, the function is constant and the image is a point.

roles.why: A nonempty interval is needed for the extreme value theorem to give a minimum.
Both cited theorems require continuity on the interval.

steps.slogan: Attain the extreme values of $f$ on the compact interval.
steps.detail: By the extreme value theorem there are $c, d \in [a, b]$ with $f(c) = m \le f(x) \le M = f(d)$ for all $x \in [a, b]$. So $f([a,b]) \subseteq [m, M]$, and both ends are values of $f$.

steps.slogan: Join the two extreme points by the intermediate value theorem.
steps.detail: Let $t \in [m, M]$. On the closed interval between $c$ and $d$, the continuous $f$ takes the values $m$ and $M$ at its ends, so some point there has the value $t$. If $c = d$ then $m = M = t$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the image is exactly $[m, M]$.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives $f([a,b]) \subseteq [m, M]$, and step 2 shows that every point of $[m, M]$ is a value. Hence $f([a,b]) = [m, M]$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity is what makes the image connected and compact.
concepts.c:closed-interval: The domain and the image are closed intervals.

source.note: The textbook route that combines the two named theorems, as in Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, chapter 4.

statement: Let the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) be split into finitely many classes. Then one class contains an IP set: all [finite sums](c:finite-sum) of distinct terms of some infinite sequence $b_0, b_1, \dots$ of positive integers.

hypotheses.text: The set of classes is finite.
Every positive integer lies in some class.

conclusion: Some class contains every sum $b_{i_1} + \dots + b_{i_k}$ with $i_1 < \dots < i_k$, for an infinite sequence $(b_i)$.

formal.difference: mathlib proves the strong form for any semigroup: a finite cover of the set of finite products of a given sequence $a$ has a part that contains such a set for a new sequence. The case here is the additive semigroup of positive integers with $a = (1, 2, 3, \dots)$, whose finite sums are all positive integers.

proofs.name: Idempotent ultrafilter
proofs.slogan: Take an idempotent ultrafilter, choose the class that belongs to it, and build the sequence term by term inside that class.
proofs.scope: The positive integers; the same argument works in any semigroup. Only the existence of an idempotent ultrafilter uses a choice principle.

roles.why: An ultrafilter that contains a finite union contains one of the members.
The union of the classes is the whole set, which belongs to every ultrafilter.

steps.slogan: Extend addition to the [ultrafilters](c:ultrafilter) on the positive integers.
steps.detail: Put $A \in U + V$ when $\{m : \{m' : m + m' \in A\} \in V\} \in U$. This makes the space $\beta\mathbb{N}$ of ultrafilters (see [Stone-Čech compactification](c:stone-cech-compactification)) a compact Hausdorff [semigroup](c:semigroup) in which $U \mapsto U + V$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Find an [idempotent](c:idempotent) ultrafilter $U$ with $U + U = U$.
steps.detail: Zorn's lemma gives a minimal closed subsemigroup $K$ of $\beta\mathbb{N}$. A short argument inside $K$ (the Ellis-Numakura lemma) shows that $K$ has an element $U$ with $U + U = U$.

steps.slogan: Choose the class that belongs to the ultrafilter $U$.
steps.detail: The classes cover the positive integers, so their union lies in $U$. An ultrafilter that contains a finite union contains one of its members, so some class $C$ belongs to $U$.

steps.slogan: Choose the terms $b_n$ one after another inside the class $C$.
steps.detail: Put $C_0 = C$. Given $C_n \in U$, the idempotent property gives an element $b_n \in C_n$ with $\{m : b_n + m \in C_n\} \in U$. Set $C_{n+1} = C_n \cap \{m : b_n + m \in C_n\}$, which is again in $U$ and shrinks.

steps.slogan: Check by induction that every sum of distinct terms lies in $C$.
steps.detail: Claim: if $i_1 < \dots < i_k$ then $b_{i_1} + \dots + b_{i_k} \in C_{i_1}$. For $k = 1$, $b_{i_1} \in C_{i_1}$. For $k > 1$, the tail sum lies in $C_{i_2} \subseteq C_{i_1 + 1} \subseteq \{m : b_{i_1} + m \in C_{i_1}\}$, so the full sum lies in $C_{i_1} \subseteq C$.

concepts.c:natural-number: The classes split the natural numbers, and the sums are taken in them.
concepts.c:finite-sum: The IP set consists of the finite sums of distinct terms.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: An ultrafilter picks one class and a large set to build from.
concepts.c:semigroup: Addition makes the positive integers a semigroup whose ultrafilters inherit a product.
concepts.c:idempotent: An idempotent ultrafilter satisfies $U + U = U$, which drives the construction.
concepts.c:stone-cech-compactification: The space of ultrafilters is the compactification that carries the extended addition.

source.note: mathlib takes an idempotent ultrafilter containing the FP set (exists_idempotent_ultrafilter_le_FP), picks the class in it (Ultrafilter.finite_sUnion_mem_iff) and builds the sequence in exists_FP_of_large.

statement: Let $C$ be a [small category](c:small-category), $F$ a [presheaf](c:presheaf) and $G$ a [copresheaf](c:copresheaf) on $C$. Put $O(F)(c) = \mathrm{Nat}(F, C(-,c))$ and $\mathrm{Spec}(G)(c) = \mathrm{Nat}(G, C(c,-))$. Then $\mathrm{Nat}(G, O(F)) \cong \mathrm{Nat}(F, \mathrm{Spec}(G))$ naturally, so $O$ is left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) to $\mathrm{Spec}$ between presheaves and opposite copresheaves.

hypotheses.text: The category $C$ is a [small category](c:small-category).
The functor $F\colon C^{op} \to \mathrm{Set}$ is a [presheaf](c:presheaf) and $G\colon C \to \mathrm{Set}$ is a [copresheaf](c:copresheaf).

conclusion: There is a bijection $\mathrm{Nat}(G, O(F)) \cong \mathrm{Nat}(F, \mathrm{Spec}(G))$, natural in $F$ and $G$, so $O \dashv \mathrm{Spec}$.

proofs.name: Families of pairings
proofs.slogan: Both sides are the set of families of maps $F(c) \times G(d) \to C(c, d)$ that are natural in $c$ and in $d$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, including the functoriality of $O$ and $\mathrm{Spec}$ and the naturality of the bijection. Smallness of $C$ makes each class of natural transformations a set.

roles.why: Smallness makes the classes $\mathrm{Nat}(F, C(-,c))$ sets, so $O(F)$ and $\mathrm{Spec}(G)$ are set-valued.
The variance of $F$ and $G$ decides how the naturality squares of a transformation read.

steps.slogan: Make $O$ and $\mathrm{Spec}$ into functors between presheaves and opposite copresheaves.
steps.detail: A morphism $f\colon c \to c'$ acts on $O(F)(c) = \mathrm{Nat}(F, C(-,c))$ by postcomposition, so $O(F)$ is a copresheaf. A map $F' \to F$ acts by precomposition $O(F) \to O(F')$, so $O$ reverses arrows. The same holds for $\mathrm{Spec}$ with $C(c,-)$.

steps.slogan: Describe the [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation) $F \to \mathrm{Spec}(G)$ as families of morphisms.
steps.detail: Such a transformation sends $x \in F(c)$ to a natural transformation $G \to C(c,-)$, that is, to morphisms $\varphi(x, y) \in C(c, d)$ for $y \in G(d)$. Naturality gives $\varphi(x, G(g)y) = g \circ \varphi(x, y)$ and $\varphi(F(f)x, y) = \varphi(x, y) \circ f$.

steps.slogan: Describe the natural transformations $G \to O(F)$ as the same families of morphisms.
steps.detail: Such a transformation sends $y \in G(d)$ to a natural transformation $F \to C(-,d)$, that is, to morphisms $\psi(x, y) \in C(c, d)$ for $x \in F(c)$. Naturality in $d$ gives $\psi(x, G(g)y) = g \circ \psi(x, y)$, and naturality in $c$ gives $\psi(F(f)x, y) = \psi(x, y) \circ f$. These are the same two rules.

steps.slogan: Check that the bijection is natural to conclude that $O$ is left [adjoint](c:adjoint-functor) to $\mathrm{Spec}$.
steps.detail: Both descriptions give the same set of families $\varphi_{c,d}\colon F(c) \times G(d) \to C(c,d)$. Maps $F' \to F$ and $G' \to G$ act only on the arguments $x$ and $y$, so the bijection commutes with them. Hence it is natural in $F$ and $G$, which is the adjunction $O \dashv \mathrm{Spec}$.

concepts.c:small-category: Smallness makes the natural transformations form sets.
concepts.c:presheaf: The presheaf $F$ is one of the two variables of the adjunction.
concepts.c:copresheaf: The copresheaf $G$ is the other variable of the adjunction.
concepts.c:adjoint-functor: The statement is an adjunction between presheaves and opposite copresheaves.
concepts.c:natural-transformation: Both sides of the bijection are sets of natural transformations.

source.note: The end calculation behind Isbell conjugation; J. R. Isbell, Adequate subcategories, Illinois Journal of Mathematics 4 (1960), 541-552, and the nLab page on Isbell duality.

statement: Let $U$, $V$ and $W$ be smooth [vector fields](c:vector-field) on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$, with [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket) $[\cdot, \cdot]$. Then $[U, [V, W]] = [[U, V], W] + [V, [U, W]]$.

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold).
The sections $U$, $V$ and $W$ are smooth [vector fields](c:vector-field) on $M$.

conclusion: The Lie bracket of vector fields satisfies the Jacobi identity in its Leibniz form.

formal.difference: mathlib assumes $C^2$ vector fields on a $C^3$ manifold modelled on a complete normed space over a nontrivially normed field, which includes the smooth real case. It states the equality of the sections as functions on $M$.

proofs.name: Chart computation
proofs.slogan: Compute in a chart, where the bracket is $DW\cdot V - DV\cdot W$; the second derivatives cancel by symmetry and the first-order terms regroup.
proofs.scope: The identity at one point $x \in M$. The bracket on a manifold is defined chartwise, so the proof reduces to a normed space.

roles.why: Charts of the [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) reduce the identity at $x$ to the model vector space.
Twice differentiable fields allow the product rule and give symmetric second derivatives.

steps.slogan: Pull the three fields back to the model space through a chart at $x$.
steps.detail: The bracket at $x$ is defined by pulling the fields back through the extended chart at $x$, taking the vector-space bracket and pushing forward. The bracket commutes with pullback by a diffeomorphism (mathlib: mpullback_mlieBracket), so every bracket in the identity is computed in the same chart for the pulled-back fields $U', V', W'$.

steps.slogan: Write the bracket of vector fields on a vector space as $DW \cdot V - DV \cdot W$.
steps.detail: In a normed space the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket) is $[V, W](y) = DW(y)\,V(y) - DV(y)\,W(y)$, where $D$ is the derivative. For $C^2$ fields both terms are $C^1$, so brackets of brackets are defined.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the bracket formula with the product rule and the chain rule.
steps.detail: For $C^2$ fields, $D\big(y \mapsto DW(y)V(y)\big)(h) = DW\,DV\,h + D^2W(h, V)$. Applying this to each term expands $[U,[V,W]]$, $[[U,V],W]$ and $[V,[U,W]]$ into products of first derivatives plus terms with one second derivative.

steps.slogan: Cancel the second-derivative terms by their symmetry.
steps.detail: The left side has the [second derivative](c:second-derivative) terms $D^2W(U, V) - D^2V(U, W)$. The right side has $D^2W(V,U) - D^2V(W,U) + D^2U(W,V) - D^2U(V,W)$. A $C^2$ map has a symmetric second derivative, so the $D^2U$ terms cancel and the right side equals the left.

steps.slogan: Match the first-derivative terms on both sides to finish the identity.
steps.detail: The left side gives $DW\,DV\,U - DV\,DW\,U + DU\,DV\,W - DU\,DW\,V$. On the right, the terms $\mp DW\,DU\,V$ and $\mp DV\,DU\,W$ cancel in pairs and leave the same four terms. So both sides agree at $x$, and $x$ was arbitrary.

concepts.c:vector-field: The identity is stated for three vector fields.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Charts of the manifold reduce the identity to a vector space.
concepts.c:lie-bracket: The bracket is the operation whose Jacobi identity is proved.
concepts.c:second-derivative: Second derivatives appear and cancel by their symmetry.

source.note: mathlib reduces to a chart with mpullback_mlieBracketWithin, then proves leibniz_identity_lieBracketWithin from the product rule (fderivWithin_clm_apply) and symmetry of second derivatives (IsSymmSndFDerivWithinAt), and closes with abel.
